episode_title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life)

stories.topic: The Bookshop Romeo (Approach With Positive EV)
stories.summary: From Amit's old Economic Times poker column 'Range Rover.' A young man walks into a bookshop, his favourite author is Milan Kundera, and across the aisle he sees a pretty girl reading Milan Kundera. Should he walk over? Even if you assume only a 10% chance she'll come out for a date and a 1% chance she's your soulmate, the value of those events is enormous and the cost of rejection is essentially zero — a moment of embarrassment. The risk-reward ratio is crazy. It is massively plus EV.
stories.insight: We make these calculations intuitively all the time without naming them. Naming the framework — expected value — lets you notice when fear of a small embarrassment is masking a near-free shot at something life-changing.

stories.topic: Bet On The Side Batting Second
stories.summary: In 2016, a poker-player friend asked Amit for an IPL betting tip. Amit told him: every match, just bet on the side batting second, no matter the price. The friend ignored him. Fourteen matches later, thirteen had been won by the chasing side — by an average of three-and-a-half wickets in seventeen-something overs. The reason wasn't just the chasing-side information advantage; it was that captains batting first, including Virat Kohli, were systematically underestimating the par score because they were stuck in the older grammar of the game.
stories.insight: When the underlying game changes, everyone keeps using the old map for years. Big edges sit there in plain sight, but pointing them out gets you abused, not paid — which is precisely why the edge persists.

stories.topic: Amla and AB de Villiers Defending For A Draw
stories.summary: On 6 December 2015 in Delhi, South Africa needed about 481 runs in a day and a half against India on a turning track. The match was effectively unwinnable. Hashim Amla scored 25 in 244 balls; AB de Villiers, one of the most aggressive batsmen ever, scored 43 in 297. Critics called it pointless, 'not how you play cricket.' But on that pitch the expected value of aggression was zero — there was no reward to extract from a risk — and the value of a wicket was infinite. They simply did the right thing for the team.
stories.insight: The 'right' decision can look ugly, slow, even cowardly to spectators if they haven't done the EV math. The willingness to do the unglamorous correct thing while the audience boos is itself a skill — and a rare one.

stories.topic: England Realised ODI Cricket Had Been Played Wrong For Three Decades
stories.summary: Around 2015-16, England's ODI side concluded that the entire cricket world had been playing one-day cricket wrong since the format began — under-aggressive in the middle overs. They started front-loading their batting (a term Amit coined in 2014). Three-hundred-plus scores went from anomalies outside the subcontinent to routine. It culminated in the 2019 World Cup win. Brendan McCullum then carried the same lens into Test cricket as England's coach — what the press christened 'Bazball' — though McCullum himself dislikes the label and insists it isn't 'all crash and burn.' The point isn't aggression for its own sake; it's getting expected value right.
stories.insight: An entire global sport spent thirty years suboptimising because no one ran the numbers. Whenever you find yourself asking 'why hasn't anyone done this?', the answer is often: because tradition feels like reasoning, and the people in the game are the ones least incentivised to question it.

stories.topic: Johnny Von Neumann Tries To Crack The Coin Toss
stories.summary: Decades ago, John von Neumann ('Johnny to all his good friends') wondered whether a coin toss is genuinely random or just Newtonian mechanics we haven't bothered to solve. He worked out heuristics that, given some initial facts about the coin, gave roughly a 0.66/0.33 edge on which face it lands. More recently, Persi Diaconis led a global project tossing physical coins millions of times — the upshot is that a coin tossed starting heads-up lands heads about 51% of the time. If you ever need to cheat at an important life decision, magnanimously offer the other person 'tails' on a coin toss.
stories.insight: Even apparently irreducible randomness usually has structure inside it if you look hard enough. The deterministic universe pokes through the probabilistic veneer in the most ordinary places — including the coin in your pocket.

stories.topic: You Are Always Speculating With Your Human Capital
stories.summary: When Ajay was leaving college, he'd argue with classmates who thought stock-picking was reckless gambling. His framing: imagine you had to pick whether steel or software would do better over the next thirty years. That's exactly the bet you're already making when you choose an industry, a company, a trade. You're staking your single biggest, least-diversifiable asset — your own human capital — on an unknowable thirty-year forecast. The 80s engineer who stumbled into Indian pharma or Indian software didn't 'know'; they got lucky and then we lionised them as great men.
stories.insight: The respectable middle-class life isn't risk-free — it's a maximally concentrated, maximally illiquid bet you make once and can't unwind. Calling stock-trading 'speculation' while pretending career choice isn't is one of the deeper self-deceptions of polite society.

recommendations.item: Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction
recommendations.creator: Philip Tetlock and Dan Gardner
recommendations.context: Tetlock's book on the people who consistently make better predictions than experts.
recommendations.reason: A masterful primer on probabilistic thinking. Amit had once thought of writing his own book on what poker taught him about thinking in probabilities and felt Superforecasting already said it all. The deeper lesson: TV experts are incentivised to exude certainty, but the world is complex; the people who genuinely think well are the ones humble enough to keep updating priors and refuse certainty when none is warranted.

recommendations.item: Thinking Strategically: The Competitive Edge in Business, Politics, and Everyday Life
recommendations.creator: Avinash Dixit and Barry Nalebuff
recommendations.context: Dixit and Nalebuff's classic on game theory for the real world.
recommendations.reason: Takes the body of game-theory knowledge from von Neumann onwards and brings it close to real-world application. Ajay's view: anyone grappling with reality will benefit. 'Strategic' here means thinking about other minds anticipating your moves — not corporate-speak.

recommendations.item: A First Course in Probability
recommendations.creator: Sheldon Ross
recommendations.context: The standard introductory probability textbook.
recommendations.reason: Mentioned by Ajay as the rigorous companion to the cricket-and-poker conversation. For the reader willing to do the math under the intuitions discussed in the episode.

recommendations.item: What Cricket Can Learn From Poker
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2016 Cricket Monthly piece — a foundational essay for the episode.
recommendations.reason: Where Amit first laid out the EV-and-cricket argument. Includes the football analogy: managers and players know the granular probabilities (Messi's 12.1% from outside the box vs 8% on a free kick) and it all gets drilled into them; cricket only began catching up with T20.

recommendations.item: What Cricket Can Learn From Economics
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2016 companion piece applying opportunity-cost reasoning to T20.
recommendations.reason: Spells out the economic logic behind front-loading. Every dot ball is a foregone alternative; in T20 the constraint is balls, not wickets; therefore aggression is the rational default.

recommendations.item: Resources vs Constraints: Why T20 Teams Need to Attack More
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2019 piece, listed in the show's 'essential reading.'
recommendations.reason: Crisply lays out the wickets-as-resource, balls-as-constraint inversion that flips T20 strategy and is still misunderstood by most teams and most commentators.

recommendations.item: Luck is All Around
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the underestimated role of luck in life.
recommendations.reason: The life-side companion to the EV argument: outcomes are heavily probabilistic, so don't let good luck make you arrogant or bad luck make you defeatist. Sweat what you can control; ignore what you can't.

recommendations.item: We Are All Gamblers
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A 2010 column rehabilitating the word 'gambler.'
recommendations.reason: Every romantic, financial, or career choice is implicitly a probabilistic judgement. Calling people who play poker or trade stocks 'gamblers' while pretending you aren't one is a category error — gambling is the human condition above the API.

recommendations.item: The Bookshop Romeo
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The first column in Amit's Range Rover series for the Economic Times (2014).
recommendations.reason: The original telling of the Milan Kundera bookshop EV calculation — high reward, near-zero downside, you should always approach. A small case study you can carry around as a portable framework.

recommendations.item: Range Rover (poker column archive)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's archived Economic Times poker column.
recommendations.reason: A pun on poker 'ranges' and the car he couldn't afford. The full archive of his roughly year-long column applying poker reasoning to everyday life.

recommendations.item: Unlikely is Inevitable
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the law of truly large numbers.
recommendations.reason: Given a large enough sample, any unlikely event must occur. Helps inoculate against the gambler's fallacy: ten tails in a row don't mean the coin is broken — they mean the sample is finally large.

recommendations.item: The Lesson From This IPL: Front-Load Your Innings
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2014 ESPN Cricinfo piece where he coined 'front-loading.'
recommendations.reason: The original frontloading argument for T20: don't preserve wickets for the death; attack from ball one because the ratio of resources to constraints demands it.

recommendations.item: Never Mind the Bullocks, Here's the Lamborghini
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2015 piece on the changed grammar of T20 cricket.
recommendations.reason: An extension of the front-loading argument as the new orthodoxy started to take hold.

recommendations.item: The New Face of Cricket
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2015 essay on how T20 has reshaped cricket.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show's resources for readers who want the longer arc of how T20 changed batting, bowling, captaincy, and selection economics.

recommendations.item: National Highway 420 (and the EV of Aggressive Batting)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2016 piece making the EV-of-aggression argument explicit.
recommendations.reason: Names the EV framework directly in a cricket context — useful primary source for the episode's central claim.

recommendations.item: The Winning Mantra for this IPL: Attack, Attack, Attack
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2017 piece doubling down on T20 aggression.
recommendations.reason: Successive seasons made the EV-of-aggression case more empirically loud — this column is the second-wave statement.

recommendations.item: For This Brave New World of Cricket, We Have IPL and England to Thank
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2019 piece on England's transformation of ODI cricket.
recommendations.reason: The praise piece for England and the IPL as the two engines that finally dragged cricket out of its three-decade ODI suboptimum and toward proper EV-based play.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: An older Amit column listed in the show resources.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Mohit Satyanand
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier deep dive on poker and markets with Mohit Satyanand.

recommendations.item: Fair Coins Tend to Land On The Same Side They Started
recommendations.creator: Frantisek Bartos et al.
recommendations.context: The arXiv paper from the Diaconis-inspired global coin-toss study.
recommendations.reason: The empirical primary source for the 51%-same-side finding Ajay cites. A reminder that even the most boring deterministic objects hide structure inside what we call randomness.

recommendations.item: eventstudies (R package)
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: An open-source R package Ajay co-authored.
recommendations.reason: Half-joking pitch to gentle readers: if you want to test whether a six in T20 actually shifts the bowler's psyche over the next few balls, an event study is exactly the right tool — and the code already exists.

core_ideas.concept: Expected Value (EV) and the Sin of Results-Oriented Thinking
core_ideas.explanation: EV is the average outcome of a decision over many trials, weighted by probability. A plus-EV bet is one you should take every time even if you sometimes lose, and a minus-EV bet is one you should never take even when you win. The deepest implication is psychological: you cannot judge the quality of a decision by its outcome, because the world is probabilistic and noisy. The amateur sees the result; the professional sees the process. Most public commentary — on cricket, policy, politics, markets — is just retroactive results-oriented thinking dressed up as analysis.
core_ideas.quote: Don't judge a policy by an outcome.

core_ideas.explanation: Every flip of a coin, every ball bowled, every decision, splits the world into branches. Once an event has happened it is 100% or 0% in your branch — but before it happens, it is a probability spread across all possible branches. Which branch you end up in is luck. The implication: evaluate decisions by the algorithm that produced them, not by the universe you happened to land in. This is the antidote to both arrogance (when lucky) and despair (when unlucky).

core_ideas.concept: Resources vs Constraints (Why T20 Demands Aggression)
core_ideas.explanation: In Test cricket, the binding constraint is wickets and the resource is balls — so defence is rational. In T20, the binding constraint is balls (only 120 of them) and the resource is wickets (you have ten regardless). Per-ball opportunity cost goes way up; the cost of a dot ball spikes; the value of a wicket falls. The expected value of aggression therefore rises sharply. Teams that imported the older ODI grammar into T20 — pinch, consolidate, slog — were committing what Ajay calls a quintessential category error: applying one domain's best practice to another without re-running the constraint math.
core_ideas.quote: Conservatism in T20 is mathematically illiterate.

core_ideas.concept: Strike Rate Minus Required Strike Rate (The Right Cricket Metric)
core_ideas.explanation: The traditional batting average is a near-useless statistic in T20. What matters is whether a batsman's strike rate exceeds the par rate his team needed to win that match. If a batsman scores 90 at 130 when 140 was needed, he hasn't helped — he has shifted the burden to the rest of the team, and a pile of such 'big' innings can be a season-long liability. Selectors who reward aggregate runs distort the entire incentive structure upstream, which is why the wrong sort of player keeps getting picked.
core_ideas.quote: If a batsman makes 900 runs in an IPL season at a strike rate below what his team needed, that's not a triumph — it's a disaster.

core_ideas.concept: The Principal-Agent Problem In Cricket Teams
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's organisational lens: every team has a gap between what makes the individual look good and what maximises the team's probability of winning. The media counting averages; selectors rewarding consistency; batsmen chasing personal landmarks — these are misaligned incentives. The fix has to come upstream, from selectors and HR-equivalents who change the metric on which players are judged. A star trader hired for the wrong KPIs is the bank's fault, not the trader's; same with a star batsman picked for the wrong reasons.

core_ideas.concept: Above the API vs Below the API
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's frame for kinds of work. Below the API life is mechanical and deterministic — the Uber driver receives a deterministic instruction (take this passenger from A to B) and is judged on compliance. Above the API life is speculative — surgeons choosing diagnostic pathways, financiers placing capital, podcasters deciding whether to make a new show. The interesting and important parts of the world are all above the API. To live a life that avoids speculation is to live below it.
core_ideas.quote: If you wish to banish speculation from your life, then you'll probably have a very dull life.

core_ideas.explanation: In polite Indian middle-class company, 'speculation' is taboo — wise grown-up people supposedly don't speculate. Ajay's argument: every interesting thing in the world involves speculation. A surgeon picking a path, an entrepreneur picking an industry, a couple deciding to move cities — all imponderable, all uncertain, all consequential. The cult of safety is itself a speculation, just an undiversified and badly-considered one. Speculate openly and well, rather than secretly and badly.

core_ideas.concept: Your Career Is Your Biggest Undiversifiable Bet
core_ideas.explanation: The 'safe' employee who refuses to trade stocks is in fact concentrating their entire human capital — their largest asset and their most illiquid one — into a single industry over a thirty-year horizon. The Indian-software and Indian-pharma generation looked like geniuses in retrospect, but at the choosing moment the future was unknowable; many of them simply got lucky. The corollary: the great-man theory of business success is mostly survivorship bias dressed up as wisdom.

core_ideas.concept: Why The Skill in Poker Hides Behind Luck
core_ideas.explanation: If you play 100 games of tennis against Nadal, you lose 100. If you play 100 games of chess against Magnus Carlsen, you lose 100. But the world's best poker player against a beginner is closer to 51-49 over a single hand. Skill exists, but the variance is enormous and the sample size required for skill to express itself is huge. The lesson generalises far beyond the felt: many professions, especially investing and entrepreneurship, are domains where short runs are dominated by luck and only the long run reveals skill — so be wary of TV experts whose track record fits inside the variance.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Ask An Economist To Forecast
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's diagnosis of a dysfunctional dynamic: the real world wants economists to be super-forecasters; economists who do their jobs honestly answer 'I don't know, it's a coin toss,' which makes the audience feel cheated. The escape is to refuse the forecasting game entirely and instead have a more interesting conversation about the forces at work, the mechanisms in motion, the scenarios on the table. Truman wanted a one-handed economist; he was demanding a worse economist.
core_ideas.quote: Living with randomness — that is the meaning of understanding finance.

core_ideas.concept: Adapting Grammar Slowly: Why New Games Are Played Wrong For Decades
core_ideas.explanation: When ODI cricket arrived, teams played it like Test cricket (Gavaskar's 36 not out off 174 balls in the 1975 World Cup). When T20 arrived, teams played it like ODIs (pinch-consolidate-slog). Even when the underlying maths flips, human institutions take a long time to update — selectors, fans, writers all reinforce the old grammar. The same lag almost certainly applies in finance, policy, and management whenever the underlying constraints shift; Amit's plea is to ask, when seeing an old mental model, whether the constraints behind it still hold.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's mock-defamatory introduction of Amit: that he secretly reads German philosophers at night. Amit's deadpan: 'I confess I read German philosophers, but that's not something one admits in public.'
Ajay, on John von Neumann: 'Many years ago, Johnny — Johnny to all his good friends — there's only one Johnny in the world, and that's Johnny von Neumann.'
Ajay's coin-toss life hack: 'Whenever you want to cheat at important life decisions, magnanimously offer the other person tails — you've just given yourself a 51-49 edge.'
Amit asking, with sheepish honesty for the gentle listeners: 'I might get kicked out of your circle of friends for asking, but what the fuck is an API?'
Amit's column was called 'Range Rover' — a pun on poker 'ranges' and the car he couldn't afford.

Amit's third possible outcome of a sky-shot in cricket, alongside 'six' and 'caught': 'the ball hits a bird in the sky and then drops down on a fielder's head, and the bird and the fielder die. Incredibly unlikely, but a non-zero possibility.'

Ajay's brushes with greatness: he watched Sunil Gavaskar bat as a child at Brabourne Stadium, and Sachin Tendulkar grew up about fifty metres away from him in Bandra East. Amit, deadpan: 'A day should come when Sachin Tendulkar says — I grew up in the same neighbourhood as Ajay Shah. I'd like that day to come.'

Bazball — coined by Andrew Miller (Amit's ex-colleague at Cricinfo) for the aggressive Test-match approach Brendan McCullum (nicknamed 'Baz') brought to England as coach. McCullum himself dislikes the term: 'I don't really like that silly term. It's not just all crash and burn.'

Harry Truman: 'Give me a one-handed economist!' — exasperated by advisors who would say 'on one hand this, on the other hand that.' Invoked here against the unrealistic demand for forecasting certainty.
Winston Churchill's lament that if you ask one economist for an opinion you get two — and three if it's John Maynard Keynes.
The Persi Diaconis-led global coin-toss project: millions of physical coin flips by researchers around the world found that a tossed coin lands on the same side it started about 51% of the time.
Brendan McCullum, the New Zealand batsman turned England Test coach, nicknamed 'Baz' — the namesake of 'Bazball.'
